nodes.statement:
{(ii)} By the proof of \eqref{l4-2-3} (also see \cite[Theorem 2.4]{CZ}), it holds that
\begin{equation} | {\mathcal L}^zp^z(t-s,x-z)|\preceq \rho^{z,0}_0(t-s,x-z),
\end{equation} and so we can verify that for every $0<s<t<1$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$,
$$\int_{\mathds R^d}| {\mathcal L}^z p^z(t-s,x-z)||q(s,z,y)|\,dz<\infty.$$
Thus, by the dominated convergence theorem, for every $0<s<t$ and $x,y \in \mathds R^d$,
\begin{equation} \begin{split}
\partial_t \phi(t,s,x,y)&=\int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L}^zp^z(t-s,x-z)q(s,z,y)\,dz\\
&=\int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L}^zp^z(t-s,x-z)(q(s,z,y)-q(s,x,y))\,dz\\
&\quad +q(s,x,y)\int_{\mathds R^d}( {\mathcal L}^z- {\mathcal L}^x)p^z(t-s,x-z)\,dz\\
&\quad +q(s,x,y)\int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L}^x p^z(t-s,x-z)\,dz\\
&=:\tilde J_1+ \tilde J_2+ \tilde J_3.
\end{split}
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{t4-1-4} with \eqref{p3-1-1a} yields that for any $0<\gamma<\theta<{\beta_0}/{\alpha_2}$,
\begin{align*}
|\tilde J_1| &\preceq \int_{\mathds R^d}\tilde \rho^{z,\tilde \theta}_0(t-s,x-z)\cdot
\tilde \rho^{y,0}_{\theta-\gamma+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})}(s,z-y)\,dz\\
&\quad +\int_{\mathds R^d}\tilde \rho^{z,\tilde \theta}_0(t-s,x-z)\cdot
\tilde \rho^{y,0}_{\theta-\gamma+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})}(s,x-y)\,dz\\
&=:\tilde J_{11}+ \tilde J_{12},
\end{align*}
where $\tilde \theta:=\alpha_1(\beta_0-\alpha_2\theta)/{\alpha_2}$.
According to \eqref{l3-2-1} (which holds for $\tilde \rho$), we obtain that
for every ${t}/{2}\leqslant s \leqslant t$,
\begin{align*}
\tilde J_{11}&\preceq \tilde \rho^{y,0}_0(t,x-y)\cdot\big[(t-s)^{-1+({\tilde \theta}/{\alpha_2})}s^{\theta-\gamma+(\beta_0/\alpha_2)-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})-1}\big]\preceq t^{-\gamma-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})-({d}/{\alpha_1})-2}(t-s)^{-1+({\tilde \theta}/{\alpha_2})},
\end{align*}
where in the last inequality we have used the fact that $\tilde\rho^{y,0}_0(t,x-y)\preceq t^{-1-d/\alpha_1}$ and
$s^{-1}\preceq t^{-1}$ for ${t}/{2}\leqslant s \leqslant t$. Note that $\tilde \rho^{y,\beta_0}_{\theta-\gamma-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})}(s,x-y)\preceq t^{-\gamma-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}$ for
every ${t}/{2}\leqslant s \leqslant t$,
and \eqref{l3-1-1} holds for $\tilde \rho$, then we have
\begin{align*}
\tilde J_{12}& \preceq t^{-\gamma-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}\int_{\mathds R^d}\tilde \rho^{z,\tilde \theta}_{0}(t-s,x-z)\,dz\preceq t^{-\gamma-({\beta_0}/{\alpha_1})-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}(t-s)^{-1+({\tilde \theta}/{\alpha_2})}.
\end{align*}

By \eqref{l2-1-2} and \eqref{p3-1-1}, we arrive at that for any $0<\gamma<\theta<{\beta_0}/{\alpha_2}$ and every
${t}/{2}\leqslant s \leqslant t$,
\begin{equation*}
|( {\mathcal L}^z- {\mathcal L}^x)p^z(t-s,x-z)|\preceq
|q_0(t-s,x, z)|\preceq \rho^{z,\beta_0}_{-\gamma}(t-s,x-z)
\end{equation*} and \begin{equation*}
|q(s,x,y)|\preceq \big(\rho^{y,0}_{({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma}+\rho^{y,\beta_0}_{-\gamma}\big)(s,x-y)\preceq t^{-\gamma-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}.
\end{equation*}
Hence, combining both estimates above with \eqref{l3-1-1},  we obtain
\begin{align*}
|\tilde J_{2}|&\preceq t^{-\gamma-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}\int_{\mathds R^d} \rho^{z,\beta_0}_{-\gamma}(t-s,x-z)\,dz
 \preceq t^{-\gamma-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}(t-s)^{-1+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma}.
\end{align*}
Furthermore, \eqref{p3-1-1} and \eqref{p4-2-1} yield that for every ${t}/{2}\leqslant s \leqslant t$ and
constants $\gamma,\theta \in (0,1)$ such that $\gamma<{\theta}/{\alpha_2}$ and
$2\gamma+({\theta}/{\alpha_1})<\beta_0/\alpha_2$,
\begin{equation*}
|\tilde J_3| \preceq t^{-\gamma-({d}/{\alpha_1})-1}(t-s)^{-1+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-2\gamma-({\theta}/{\alpha_1})}.
\end{equation*}


On the other hand, when $0<s\leqslant {t}/{2}$,  it follows from \eqref{t4-1-4}, \eqref{p3-1-1} and \eqref{l3-2-1} that
\begin{align*}
\big|\partial_t \phi(t,s,x,y)\big|
 &\preceq
\int_{\mathds R^d}\big| {\mathcal L}^z p^z(t-s,x-z)\big|\big|q(s,z,y)\big|\,dz\\
&\preceq \int_{\mathds R^d} \rho^{z,0}_0(t-s,x-z)\cdot
\big(\rho^{y,0}_{({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma}+\rho^{y,\beta_0}_{-\gamma}\big)(s,z-y)\,dz\\
&\preceq \rho^{y,0}_0(t,x-y)\cdot\big[(t-s)^{-1}s^{({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma}+
(t-s)^{-1+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})}s^{-\gamma}+s^{-1+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma}\big]\\
&\quad +\rho^{y,\beta_0}_{0}(t,x-y)\cdot(t-s)^{-1}s^{-\gamma}\\
&\preceq t^{-2-({d}/{\alpha_1})}s^{-1+({\beta_0}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma},
\end{align*}
where in the last inequality we have used the facts that $\rho^{y,0}_0(t,x-y)\preceq t^{-1-({d}/{\alpha_1})}$ and $(t-s)^{-1}\preceq t^{-1}$ for every
$0<s\leqslant {t}/{2}$.
Therefore, choosing $\gamma,\theta \in (0,1)$ such that $\gamma<{\theta}/{\alpha_2}$ and
$2\gamma+({\theta}/{\alpha_1})<\beta_0/\alpha_2$, and combining all the estimates above,  we
know that \eqref{e:lkk} is well defined, and that for every $t \in (0,1)$,
$
\sup_{t_0 \in (t,t+\varepsilon_1)}|
\partial_t\phi(t_0,s,x,y)|\leqslant \eta(t,s),
$
where $\eta$ is a non-negative measurable function such that
$\int_0^t \eta(t,s)\,ds<\infty$ and $\varepsilon_1>0$ is a constant small enough (which may depend on $t$).
Now, according to the dominated convergence theorem, for every $t \in (0,1]$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$,
\begin{equation} \begin{split}
\lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\cdot
\bigg(\int_0^t \big(\phi(t+\varepsilon,s,x,y)-\phi(t,s,x,y)\big)\,ds\bigg)=
\int_0^t \partial_t \phi(t,s,x,y)\,ds.
\end{split}
\end{equation}

nodes.statement: Let $u \in C_b([0,1]\times \mathds R^d)$ be the solution of the following equation \begin{equation} {\partial_t u(t,x)}= {\mathcal L} u(t,x),\quad (t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d. \end{equation} Suppose \begin{equation} \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}\big|u(t,x)-u(0,x)\big|=0, \end{equation} and for every $x \in \mathds R^d$, $t \mapsto {\mathcal L} u(t,x)$ is continuous in $t \in (0,1]$. Assume that there exists a function $\theta(x)\in (0,1)$ such that $\inf_{x \in \mathds R^d}\big(\theta(x)+1-\alpha(x)\big)>0$ and for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, \begin{equation} \sup_{t \in (\varepsilon,1)}\big|u(t,x)-u(t,x')\big|\leqslant c_1(\varepsilon)|x-x'|^{\theta(x)},\quad x,x'\in \mathds R^d. \end{equation} Then for every $t \in (0,1]$, \begin{equation*} \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u(t,x)\leqslant \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u(0,x). \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: Throughout the proof, the constant $C$ denotes a positive constant that is independent of $R$ and $x$ whose exact value may change from line to line. Since \eqref{t4-3-1} holds, it suffices to prove that for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $t\in (\varepsilon,1]$, \begin{equation} \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u(t,x)\leqslant \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u(\varepsilon,x). \end{equation} For every $R>1$, we can choose a smooth cut-off function $l_R:\mathds R^d \rightarrow \mathds R$ such that \begin{equation*} l_R(x)= \begin{cases} 1,\ \ \ & |x|\leqslant R,\\ \in [0,1],\ & R<|x|<2R,\\ 0,\ \ \ &|x|\geqslant 2R, \end{cases} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation} |\nabla l_R(x)|^2+|\nabla^2 l_R(x)|\leqslant \frac{C}{R^2},\quad x\in \mathds R^d. \end{equation} For every $R,\delta>0$ and $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, define $$u_{R}^{\delta}(t,x)= u(t,x)l_R(x)-(t-\varepsilon)\delta,\quad x\in \mathds R^d, t\in (\varepsilon,1).$$ Then, it follows from the fact $\partial_t u(t,x)= {\mathcal L} u(t,x)$ that \begin{equation} {\partial_t u_R^{\delta}(t,x)}= {\mathcal L} u_R^{\delta}(t,x)+g_R^{\delta}(t,x), \end{equation} where $g_R^{\delta}(t,x):= {\mathcal L} u(t,x)\cdot l_R(x)-{\mathcal L}(u\cdot l_R)(t,x)-\delta$. Observe that \begin{align*} & {\mathcal L}(u\cdot l_R)(t,x)- {\mathcal L} u(t,x)\cdot l_R(x)-{\mathcal L} l_R(x)\cdot u(t,x)\\ &=\int_{\mathds R^d}(u(t,x+z)-u(t,x))\cdot (l_R(x+z)-l_R(x)) \frac{\kappa(x,z)}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\\ &\preceq \int_{\{|z|\leqslant 1\}} (u(t,x+z)-u(t,x))\cdot (l_R(x+z)-l_R(x)) \frac{1}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\\ &\quad +\int_{\{|z|> 1\}} (u(t,x+z)-u(t,x))\cdot (l_R(x+z)-l_R(x)) \frac{1}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\\ &=:J_1+J_2. \end{align*} On the one hand, by \eqref{t4-3-2} and \eqref{t4-3-6}, \begin{align*} J_1&\leqslant \frac{C(\varepsilon)}{R}\int_{\{|z|\leqslant 1\}} \frac{|z|^{1+\theta(x)}}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\leqslant \frac{C(\varepsilon)}{R}, \end{align*} where in the last inequality we used $\inf_{x \in \mathds R^d}\big(\theta(x)+1-\alpha(x)\big)>0$. On the other hand, for every $0<\gamma< \alpha_1\wedge 1$, \begin{align*} J_2&\leqslant 2\|u\|_{\infty}\|l_R\|_{\infty}^{1-\gamma} \int_{\{|z|>1\}}\frac{|l_R(x+z)-l_R(x)|^{\gamma}}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\leqslant \frac{C\|u\|_{\infty}}{R^{\gamma}}\int_{\{|z|>1\}} |z|^{-d-\alpha(x)+\gamma}\,dz\leqslant C\|u\|_{\infty}R^{-\gamma}. \end{align*} According to the argument above, it is easy to verify that $$ |{\mathcal L} l_R(x)|\leqslant CR^{-\gamma}. $$ Combining all the estimates above yields \begin{equation} \begin{split} g_R^{\delta}(t,x)\leqslant C(\varepsilon,u)R^{-\gamma}-\delta. \end{split} \end{equation} Now we are going to verify that for every fixed $R$ large enough, \begin{equation} \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u_R^{\delta}(t,x)\leqslant \sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}u_R^{\delta}(\varepsilon,x),\quad t\in (\varepsilon,1]. \end{equation} Suppose \eqref{t4-3-7} does not hold. Then for every large enough $R$, there exists $(t_0,x_0) \in (\varepsilon,1]\times \mathds R^d$ (which may depend on $R$, $\varepsilon$ and $\delta>0$) such that \begin{equation} \sup_{(t,x) \in (\varepsilon,1)\times\mathds R^d}u_R^{\delta}(t,x)=u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0). \end{equation} Note that the existence of $(t_0,x_0)$ follows from the fact that $u_R^{\delta}(t,x)=0$ for every $t \in (\varepsilon,1]$ and $|x|>2R$. Therefore, by \eqref{t4-3-3}, we have for every $h \in (0,t_0-\varepsilon)$, \begin{align*} 0\leqslant \frac{u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)-u_R^{\delta}(t_0-h,x_0)}{h}= \frac{1}{h}\int_{t_0-h}^{t_0} {\mathcal L} u_R^{\delta}(s,x_0)\,ds+ \frac{1}{h}\int_{t_0-h}^{t_0}g_R^{\delta}(s,x_0)\,ds. \end{align*} Letting $h \downarrow 0$, we arrive at \begin{equation} 0\leqslant {\mathcal L} u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)+g_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0), \end{equation} thanks to the assumption that the function $t \mapsto {\mathcal L} u(t,x)$ is continuous on $(0,1]$. Furthermore, from \eqref{t4-3-7a} it is easy to see \begin{equation*} {\mathcal L} u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)=\int_{\mathds R^d}\big(u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0+z)+ u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0-z)-2u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)\big)\frac{\kappa(x_0,z)}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x_0)}}\,dz\leqslant 0. \end{equation*} Combining this with \eqref{t4-3-6a}, we get that for every $R>\big(\frac{2C(\varepsilon,u)}{\delta}\big)^{{1}/{\gamma}}$, \begin{align*} {\mathcal L} u_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)+g_R^{\delta}(t_0,x_0)\leqslant -{\delta}/{2}, \end{align*} which contradicts with \eqref{t4-3-8}. Hence, the assumption above fails and so \eqref{t4-3-7} holds. Letting $R \rightarrow \infty$ in \eqref{t4-3-7}, we obtain \eqref{t4-3-5} immediately.

nodes.statement: (i) We first assume that $\kappa(x,z)$ is independent of $z$. We will prove that $p(t,x,y)$ constructed by \eqref{eq2-1} satisfies all the assertions. According to Proposition \ref{t4-1}, \eqref{t1-1-1} holds. By Propositions \ref{p3-2} and \ref{p3-3}, \eqref{t1-1-4} and \eqref{t1-1-4a} hold true. Propositions \ref{t4-2} and \ref{t5-1} imply \eqref{t1-1-7} and \eqref{t1-1-7a}, respectively. By Proposition \ref{p4-5}, we know that $p:(0,1]\times\mathds R^d\times \mathds R^d\rightarrow \mathds R_+$ is continuous. The lower bounds \eqref{t1-1-4b} will be shown in Corollary \ref{c-lower}, which is a consequence of Propositions \ref{p4-3} and \ref{t4-4} in the next subsection. \smallskip (ii) According to the proof of Proposition \ref{t4-1}, we can obtain that for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, there exist a constant $C(\varepsilon)>0$ and a measurable function $\eta:\mathds R^d \to \mathds R_+$ such that $\int_{\mathds R^d}\eta(y)\,dy<\infty$, \begin{equation*} \sup_{t \in (\varepsilon,1)}\Big|\frac{\partial p(t,x,y)}{\partial t}\Big|\leqslant C(\varepsilon)\eta(x-y) \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*}\begin{split} &\sup_{t \in (\varepsilon,1),\sigma>0}\bigg|\int_{\{|z|>\sigma\}}\big(p(t,x+z,y)+p(t,x-z,y)-2p(t,x,y)\big) \frac{\kappa(x,z)}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\bigg|\leqslant C(\varepsilon)\eta(x-y).\end{split} \end{equation*} Thus, by the dominated convergence theorem, it is easy to verify that ${\mathcal L} u_f (t, \cdot) (x)$ exists for each $t>0$ and $x\in \mathds R^d$, $t\mapsto {\mathcal L} u_f (t, \cdot) (x)$ is continuous, and that \eqref{t1-1-2} holds. \smallskip (iii) We have by \eqref{eq2-1} that \begin{align*} u_f(t,x)-f(x)&=\int_{\mathds R^d}p^y(t,x-y)\big(f(y)-f(x)\big)\,dy+ f(x)\left(\int_{\mathds R^d}p^y(t,x-y)\,dy-1\right)\\ &\quad +\int_{\mathds R^d} f(y)\int_0^t\int_{\mathds R^d}p^z(t-s,x-z)q(s,z,y)\,dz\,ds\,dy\\ &=:J_1+J_2+J_3. \end{align*} For any $f\in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a constant $\delta:=\delta(\varepsilon)>0$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ for all $x,y \in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\leqslant \delta$. Thus, \begin{align*} |J_1|&\leqslant \int_{\{|y-x|\leqslant \delta\}}p^y(t,x-y)|f(y)-f(x)|\,dy+ \int_{\{|y-x|>\delta\}}p^y(t,x-y)|f(y)-f(x)|\,dy\\ &\leqslant \varepsilon \int_{\mathds R^d}\rho^{y,0}_1(t,x-y)\,dy+ C(\varepsilon)\|f\|_{\infty}\int_{\{|y-x|>\delta\}}\frac{t}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha_1}}\,dy\leqslant C\varepsilon+C(\varepsilon,\delta)t, \end{align*} where in the last inequality we have used \eqref{l3-1-1}. According to \eqref{p4-1-1}, it holds that $\lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}|J_2|=0$. Furthermore, by \eqref{p3-1-1} and \eqref{l3-3-1}, we obtain that for $\gamma<\beta_0^*/{\alpha_2}$ with $\beta^*\in (0,\beta]\cap(0,\alpha_2/2)$, \begin{align*} |J_3|&\preceq \|f\|_{\infty}\Bigg[\int_{\mathds R^d} \int_0^t\int_{\mathds R^d}\rho^{z,0}_1(t-s,x-z) \Big(\rho^{y,0}_{{(\beta_0^*/\alpha_2)}-\gamma}(s,z-y)+ \rho^{y,\beta_0^*}_{-\gamma}(s,z-y)\Big)\,dz\,ds\,dy\Bigg]\\ &\preceq \|f\|_{\infty}\int_{\mathds R^d} \Big(\rho^{y,0}_{1+{(\beta_0^*/\alpha_2)}-\gamma}+\rho^{y,\beta_0^*}_{1-\gamma}\Big)(t,x-y)\,dy\preceq t^{{(\beta_0^*/\alpha_2)}-\gamma}\|f\|_{\infty}. \end{align*} Combining all the estimates above together, we arrive at \begin{equation*} \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}\big|u_f(t,x)-f(x)\big|\leqslant \varepsilon. \end{equation*} Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we know that \eqref{t1-1-3} holds. \smallskip (iv) Denote by $C_{b}^{\varepsilon}(\mathds R^d)$ the set of bounded H\"{o}lder continuous functions, and by $C_{b}^{2,\varepsilon}(\mathds R^d)$ the set of bounded twice differentiable functions whose second derivatives are uniformly H\"{o}lder continuous. We first suppose that $f \in C_{b}^{2,\varepsilon}(\mathds R^d)$. Let \begin{equation*} \tilde u_f(t,x):=f(x)+\int_0^t\int_{\mathds R^d}p(s,x,y){\mathcal L} f(y)\,dy\,ds=f(x)+\int_0^t u_{{\mathcal L} f}(s,x)\,ds. \end{equation*} Since ${\mathcal L} f \in C_{b}^{\varepsilon}(\mathds R^d)$, it is easy to see that \begin{equation*} \frac{\partial \tilde u_f(t,x)}{\partial t}=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,y){\mathcal L} f(y)\,dy =u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x),\quad t\in (0,1] \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x\in\mathds R^d}|\tilde u_f(t,x)-f(x)|=0. \end{equation*} On the other hand, due to ${\mathcal L} f \in C_{b}^{\varepsilon}(\mathds R^d)$ again, it follows from \eqref{t1-1-2} that $ {\mathcal L} u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x)=\frac{\partial u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x)}{\partial t}$. Furthermore, following the proof of Proposition \ref{t4-1}, we will get \begin{align*} \int_0^t \Big|\int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L}^x p^z(t-s,x-z){\mathcal L} f(z)\,dz\Big|\,ds &\leqslant \int_0^t \Big|\int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L}^z p^z(t-s,x-z){\mathcal L} f(z)\,dz\Big|\,ds\\ &\quad +\int_0^t \Big|\int_{\mathds R^d}( {\mathcal L}^x- {\mathcal L}^z) p^z(t-s,x-z){\mathcal L} f(z)\,dz\Big|\,ds<\infty \end{align*} and so $$\int_0^t {\mathcal L} u_{{\mathcal L} f}(s,x)\,ds$$ is well defined. Hence, \begin{align*} {\mathcal L}\tilde u_f(t,x)&={\mathcal L} f(x)+\int_0^t {\mathcal L} u_{{\mathcal L} f}(s,x)\,ds={\mathcal L} f(x)+\int_0^t \frac{\partial u_{{\mathcal L} f}(s,x)}{\partial s}\,ds\\ &={\mathcal L} f(x)+u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x)-{\mathcal L} f(x)=u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x), \end{align*} where in the third equality we used $\lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x\in\mathds R^d}|u_{{\mathcal L} f}(t,x)-{\mathcal L} f(x)|=0$, thanks to \eqref{t1-1-3}. Therefore, both $u_f$ and $\tilde u_f$ are solutions of the following PDE \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \frac{\partial u(t,x)}{\partial t}= {\mathcal L} u(t,x),\\ \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}|u(t,x)-f(x)|=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} Let $w_f(t,x):=u_f(t,x)-\tilde u_f(t,x)$. Then, \eqref{t4-3-2a} and \eqref{t4-3-1} hold for $w_f$ with $w_f(0,x)\equiv 0$. At the same time, it is easy to verify from \eqref{eq2-1} that the function $t \mapsto {\mathcal L} w_f(t,x)$ is continuous on $(0,1]$, and that \eqref{t1-1-7} implies \eqref{t4-3-2} holds for $w_f$. Thus, by Theorem \ref{t4-3}, we have \begin{equation*} w_f(t,x)\leqslant w_f(0,x)=0,\quad (t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d. \end{equation*} Furthermore, applying the argument above to $-w_f$, we finally get that \begin{equation*} w_f(t,x)\equiv 0,\quad (t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d. \end{equation*} Therefore, $u_f(t,x)=\tilde u_f(t,x)$ for any $t \in (0,1]$ and $x \in \mathds R^d$, which further implies that \begin{equation*} \int_{\mathds R^d} {\mathcal L} p(t,\cdot,y)(x)f(y)\,dy=\frac{\partial u_f(t,x)}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial \tilde u_{f}(t,x)}{\partial t}=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,y){\mathcal L} f(y)\,dy. \end{equation*} Thus, \eqref{t1-1-5a} holds. Observe that \begin{equation*} u_f(t,x)=\tilde u_f(t,x)=f(x)+\int_0^t u_{{\mathcal L} f}(s,x)\,ds. \end{equation*} According to \eqref{t1-1-3}, we arrive at \eqref{t1-1-5b} immediately. By the standard approximation procedure, we know that \eqref{t1-1-5a} and \eqref{t1-1-5b} still hold for every $f \in C_{b,u}^2(\mathds R^d)$. \smallskip (v) Let $u(t,x)=:\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,y)\,dy$. Then, according to \eqref{t1-1-2} and \eqref{t1-1-3}, we know that $u$ satisfies the following equation \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \frac{\partial u(t,x)}{\partial t}= {\mathcal L} u(t,x),\\ \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}\big|u(t,x)-1\big|=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} At the same time, $v(t,x)\equiv 1$ satisfies the equation \eqref{t1-1-11} above. Note that \eqref{t4-3-2} and the time continuity condition hold for both $u(t,x)$ and $v(t,x)$. Then, using the same argument as in (iv) and applying Theorem \ref{t4-3}, we obtain \begin{equation*} \int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,y)\,dy=u(t,x)=1,\quad (t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d, \end{equation*} which is \eqref{t1-1-6}. For every fixed $s \in (0,1)$ and $y \in \mathds R^d$, we define $$u_{s,y}(t,x):=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,z)p(s,z,y)\,dz.$$ Again by \eqref{t1-1-2} and \eqref{t1-1-3}, the following equation holds for $u_{s,y}$: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \frac{\partial u_{s,y}(t,x)}{\partial t}= {\mathcal L} u_{s,y}(t,x),\\ \lim_{t \downarrow 0}\sup_{x \in \mathds R^d}|u_{s,y}(t,x)-p(s,x,y)|=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} On the other hand, it is easy to verify that $v_{s,y}(t,x):=p(t+s,x,y)$ satisfies \eqref{t1-1-12}, and \eqref{t4-3-2} and the time continuity condition hold for both $u_{s,y}(t,x)$ and $v_{s,y}(t,x)$. Following the procedure above and applying Theorem \ref{t4-3}, we arrive at $$\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,z)p(s,z,y)\,dz=u_{s,y}(t,x)=v_{s,y}(t,x)=p(t+s,x,y),$$ which is \eqref{t1-1-5}. \smallskip (vi) Suppose that $\widehat p(t,x,y)$ is another jointly continuous function on $(0, 1]\times \mathds R^d\times \mathds R^d$ that is bounded for each $t>0$ and satisfies \eqref{t1-1-7} and \eqref{t1-1-2a}-\eqref{t1-1-3}. For every $f \in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$, let $$\widehat u_f(t,x):=\int_{\mathds R^d}\widehat p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy \quad \hbox{and} \quad \widehat w_f(t,x):=u_f(t,x)-\widehat u_f(t,x). $$ Then both $u_f$ and $\widehat u_f$ satisfy \eqref{t1-1-2}. By the same argument above, we have $\widehat w_f(t,x)=0$ for each $(t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d$. This implies that for every $f \in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$, \begin{equation*} \int_{\mathds R^d} p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathds R^d} \widehat p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy. \end{equation*} Consequently, $p(t,x,y)=\widehat p(t,x,y)$ for a.e.\ $y \in \mathds R^d$ and hence for every $y\in \mathds R^d$. \smallskip (vii) Suppose that $\kappa(x,z)$ depends on $z$. The desired upper and lower estimates and the regularity can be proved in a similar way as before. On the other hand, the condition ${(\alpha_2/\alpha_1)}-1<\beta_*/\alpha_2<{1}/{2}$ implies that $\alpha_2-\alpha_1<{\alpha_1}/{2}<1$, which ensures that \eqref{t4-3-2} holds with $u_f(t,x):=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy$ for every $f \in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$. Therefore, following the arguments in steps (i)-(vi), we can verify that \eqref{t1-1-5}-\eqref{t1-1-5b} hold in such case.

(ii) According to  the proof of Proposition \ref{t4-1}, we can
obtain that for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, there exist a constant
$C(\varepsilon)>0$ and a measurable function $\eta:\mathds R^d \to  \mathds R_+$ such that
$\int_{\mathds R^d}\eta(y)\,dy<\infty$,

\begin{equation*}
\sup_{t \in (\varepsilon,1)}\Big|\frac{\partial p(t,x,y)}{\partial t}\Big|\leqslant C(\varepsilon)\eta(x-y)
\end{equation*} and
\begin{equation*}\begin{split}
&\sup_{t \in (\varepsilon,1),\sigma>0}\bigg|\int_{\{|z|>\sigma\}}\big(p(t,x+z,y)+p(t,x-z,y)-2p(t,x,y)\big)
\frac{\kappa(x,z)}{|z|^{d+\alpha(x)}}\,dz\bigg|\leqslant C(\varepsilon)\eta(x-y).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
Thus, by the dominated convergence theorem, it is easy to verify
that ${\mathcal L} u_f (t, \cdot) (x)$ exists for each $t>0$ and $x\in \mathds R^d$, $t\mapsto {\mathcal L} u_f (t, \cdot) (x)$
is continuous,  and that \eqref{t1-1-2} holds.

(vi)
Suppose that $\widehat p(t,x,y)$ is another
jointly continuous function  on $(0, 1]\times \mathds R^d\times \mathds R^d$
that is bounded for each $t>0$ and
 satisfies  \eqref{t1-1-7} and \eqref{t1-1-2a}-\eqref{t1-1-3}.
For every $f \in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$, let
$$\widehat u_f(t,x):=\int_{\mathds R^d}\widehat p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy \quad \hbox{and} \quad
\widehat w_f(t,x):=u_f(t,x)-\widehat u_f(t,x).
$$
 Then both $u_f$ and $\widehat u_f$ satisfy \eqref{t1-1-2}. By the same argument above, we have
$\widehat w_f(t,x)=0$ for each $(t,x)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d$. This implies
that for every $f \in C_{b,u}(\mathds R^d)$,
\begin{equation*}
\int_{\mathds R^d} p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathds R^d} \widehat p(t,x,y)f(y)\,dy.
\end{equation*}
Consequently, $p(t,x,y)=\widehat p(t,x,y)$ for a.e.\ $y \in \mathds R^d$ and hence for every $y\in \mathds R^d$.

nodes.statement: For simplicity, we only prove the case that $\kappa(x,z)$ depends on $z$ and $({\alpha_2}/{\alpha_1})-1<\beta_0^{**}/{\alpha_2}$, since the other case can be tackled similarly and easily. First, according to \eqref{l3-2-8}, for any $t\in(0,1]$ and $x,y\in\mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\leqslant 5 (t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\vee t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})\leqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha_2}}$, \begin{equation} t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\asymp t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}. \end{equation} It is well known that for any $t>0$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$, $$p^y(t,x-y)\asymp \frac{t}{(t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}+|x-y|)^{d+\alpha(y)}}.$$ Thus, for all $t\in (0,1]$ and $x,y\in\mathds R^d$, \begin{equation} p^y(t,x-y)\succeq t^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}} \quad\textrm{ when }|x-y|\leqslant 5(t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\vee t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}). \end{equation} Second, \eqref{p3-1-2} and \eqref{l3-3-1} yield that for all $t\in (0,1]$ and $x,y\in\mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\leqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha_2}}$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\int_0^t \int_{\mathds R^d} p^z(t-s,x-z)|q(s,z,y)|\,dz\,ds\\ &\preceq\int_0^t \int_{\mathds R^d}\rho^{z,0}_1(t-s,x-z) \cdot\Big(\rho^{y,0}_{({\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma_2 }+\rho^{y,\beta_0^{**}}_{-\gamma_2 }\Big)(s,z,y)\,dz\,ds\\ &\preceq \rho^{y,\beta_0^{**}}_{1-\gamma_2 }(t,x-y)+\rho^{y,0}_{1+({\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma_2 }(t,x-y)\\ & \preceq |x-y|^{\beta_0^{**}}t^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}-\gamma_2 }+t^{-({d}/{\alpha(y)})+({\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma_2 }\preceq t^{-({d}/{\alpha(y)})+({\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2})-\gamma_2 }, \end{split} \end{equation} where in the first inequality $\gamma_2: =({\alpha_2}/{\alpha_1})-1+\gamma$ and the fourth inequality follows from the fact that $|x-y|\leqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha_2}}$. The assumption $({\alpha_2}/{\alpha_1})-1<{\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2}$ ensures that we can choose $\gamma>0$ small enough such that $\gamma_2 <{\beta_0^{**}}/{\alpha_2}$. Combining \eqref{p4-3-4} with \eqref{p4-3-3}, \eqref{eq2-1} and \eqref{p4-3-2}, we arrive at that there is a constant $t_0\in(0,1]$ such that for all $t\in (0,t_0]$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\leqslant 5(t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\vee t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})$, \begin{equation} p(t,x,y)\succeq t^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}}\asymp t^{-{d}/{\alpha(x)}}. \end{equation} Note that, according to the argument above, \eqref{pnte} still holds for all $t\in (0,t_0]$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\preceq (t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\vee t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})$. Furthermore, due to \eqref{p4-3-2}, for any $y,z\in \mathds R^d$ with $|z-y|\leqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}$, we have $|x-z|\leqslant |z-y|+|x-y|\preceq t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}$ for any $x\in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\preceq (t^{1/\alpha(x)}\vee t^{1/\alpha(y)})$, and so $$p(t,x,z)\succeq t^{-{d}/{\alpha(z)}}\asymp t^{-{d}/{\alpha(x)}},\quad t\in (0,t_0],$$ thanks to \eqref{p4-3-2} again. Therefore, according to the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation \eqref{t1-1-5} and \eqref{pnte}, for every $t\in [t_0,2t_0]$ and $x,y\in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\leqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}$, \begin{align*} p(t,x,y)&=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(t_0,x,z)p(t-t_0,z,y)\,dz\succeq (t-t_0)^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}}\int_{\{|z-y|\leqslant 5(t-t_0)^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}\}} p(t_0,x,z)\,dz\\ &\succeq (t-t_0)^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}}t_0^{-{d}/{\alpha(x)}}(t-t_0)^{{d}/{\alpha(y)}}\succeq t^{-{d}/{\alpha(x)}}. \end{align*} Iterating the arguments above $[{1}/{t_0}]+1$ times, we can obtain \eqref{p4-3-1}.

Moreover, $X$ has the strong Feller property. $(2)$ For every non-negative measurable function $g:(0,1]\times \mathds R^d \times \mathds R^d \rightarrow \mathds R_+$ vanishing on $\{(s,x,y)\in (0,1]\times \mathds R^d \times \mathds R^d: x=y\}$ and any stopping time $T$, we have \begin{equation} \mathds E_x\left(\sum_{s \leqslant T\wedge 1}g(s,X_{s-},X_s)\right)=\mathds E_x \bigg(\int_0^{T\wedge 1}\int_{\mathds R^d} g(s,X_s,y)J(X_s,y)\,dy\,ds\bigg), \end{equation} where $$J(x,y):=\frac{\kappa(x,y-x)}{|y-x|^{d+\alpha(x)}},\quad x,y \in \mathds R^d.$$

nodes.statement: Choose a function $f \in C_b^2(\mathds R^d)$ such that $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=1$ for every $|x|\geqslant 1$. For each $r>0$ and $x \in \mathds R^d$, define $f_{r,x}(y):=f\big(\frac{y-x}{r}\big)$. Then, by \eqref{p4-4-0}, for every $0<r<1$, $A>0$ and $x \in \mathds R^d$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathds P_x \big(\tau_{B(x,Ar)}\leqslant r^{\alpha(x)}\big)&\leqslant \mathds E_x f_{Ar,x}\big(X_{\tau_{B(x,Ar)}\wedge r^{\alpha(x)}}\big)=\mathds E_x \Big(\int_0^{\tau_{B(x,Ar)}\wedge r^{\alpha(x)}}{\mathcal L} f_{Ar,x}(X_s)\,ds\Big). \end{split} \end{equation} Observe that for every $y \in B(x,Ar)$ and $\lambda>1$, \begin{align*} |{\mathcal L} f_{Ar,x}(y)|&\preceq \int_{\{|z|\leqslant \lambda r\}}|\delta_{f_{Ar,x}}(y;z)|\cdot \frac{dz}{|z|^{d+\alpha(y)}} +\int_{\{|z|>\lambda r\}}|\delta_{f_{Ar,x}}(y;z)|\cdot \frac{dz}{|z|^{d+\alpha(y)}}\\ &\preceq \frac{\|\nabla^2 f\|_{\infty}}{(Ar)^2} \int_{\{|z|\leqslant \lambda r\}}|z|^{2-d-\alpha(y)}\,dz+\|f\|_{\infty} \int_{\{|z|> \lambda r\}}|z|^{-d-\alpha(y)}\,dz\\ &\preceq \bigg(\frac{\|\nabla^2 f\|_{\infty}\lambda^{2-\alpha(y)}}{A^2}+ \frac{\|f\|_{\infty}}{\lambda^{\alpha(y)}}\bigg)\cdot r^{-\alpha(y)}. \end{align*} Hence, first taking $\lambda$ large enough and then $A$ large enough, we can find a constant $A_0>0$ such that \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal L} f_{A_0r,x}(y)|\leqslant \frac{1}{4}r^{-\alpha(y)}\quad \textrm{for all } y \in B(x,A_0r). \end{equation*} Since for every $y \in B(x,A_0r)$ and $r\in (0,1)$, \begin{align*} r^{-\alpha(y)}&=r^{-\alpha(x)}r^{-(\alpha(y)-\alpha(x))}\leqslant r^{-|\alpha(x)-\alpha(y)|}r^{-\alpha(x)}\leqslant r^{-C_1(A_0r)^{\beta_0}}r^{-\alpha(x)}\leqslant \exp(C_2|\log r|r^{\beta_0})r^{-\alpha(x)}, \end{align*} there exists a constant $r_0>0$ small enough such that $r^{-\alpha(y)}\leqslant 2 r^{-\alpha(x)}$ for all $r \in (0,r_0)$ and $y \in B(x,A_0r)$. Hence, we have for every $r \in (0,r_0)$ and $y\in B(x,A_0r)$, \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal L} f_{A_0r,x}(y)|\leqslant \frac{1}{2}r^{-\alpha(x)}. \end{equation*} Therefore, putting this estimate into \eqref{l4-3-2}, we obtain \eqref{l4-3-1}.

nodes.statement: For any $t\in (0,1]$ and $x,y\in\mathds R^d$, it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathds P_x\big(X_{\lambda t}\in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})\big)\\ &\geqslant \mathds P_x\big(\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\leqslant \lambda t; \sup_{s \in (\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)},\lambda t)}\big|X_s-X_{\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}}\big|\leqslant t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2\big)\\ &\geqslant\mathds P_x\big(\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\leqslant \lambda t ;\mathds P_{X_{\sigma_{B(y, t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}}}\big(\sup_{0\leqslant s \leqslant \lambda t}|X_s-X_0|\leqslant t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2\big)\big)\\ &\geqslant \mathds P_x\big(\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\leqslant \lambda t\big) \cdot \inf_{z \in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\mathds P_z\big( \tau_{B(z,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}>\lambda t\big), \end{split} \end{equation} where in the second inequality we have used the strong Markov property. Following the proof of \eqref{l3-2-8}, we know that $t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}\geqslant C_1 t^{{1}/{\alpha(z)}}$ for every $z \in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)$. Hence, there exists a constant $0<\lambda_0<1$ such that for all $0<\lambda<\lambda_0$ and $z \in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathds P_z\big(\tau_{B(z,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}>\lambda t\big) \geqslant \mathds P_z\big(\tau_{B(z,{C_1t^{{1}/{\alpha(z)}}}/{2})}>\lambda t\big)\geqslant {1}/{2}, \end{split} \end{equation} where the last inequality follows from \eqref{l4-3-1}. On the other hand, by the L\'evy system \eqref{p4-4-1}, for $\lambda>0$ small enough and for any $x,y\in \mathds R^d$ with $ |x-y|>5\max\{t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}},t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}\}$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathds P_x\big(\sigma_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\leqslant \lambda t\big) &\geqslant \mathds P_x\big(X_{\lambda t \wedge \tau_{B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})}}\in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)\big)\\ &=\mathds E_x\bigg(\int_0^{\lambda t \wedge \tau_{B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})}} \int_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)}\frac{du}{|X_s-u|^{d+\alpha(X_s)}}\,ds\bigg)\\ &\succeq \lambda t^{1+({d}/{\alpha(y)})}\cdot \inf_{z \in B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})}\frac{1}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha(z)}} \cdot \mathds P_x\big(\tau_{B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})}\geqslant \lambda t\big)\\ &\succeq \frac{t^{1+({d}/{\alpha(y)})}}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha(x)}}, \end{split} \end{equation} where in the first inequality we used the fact that $|x-y|\geqslant 5\max\{t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}},t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}\}$ implies $B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})\cap B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2)=\emptyset$, the second inequality follows from the fact that $|z-u|\preceq |x-y|$ for any $z \in B\big(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}\big)$ and $u \in B\big(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}/2\big)$, and in the last inequality we used \eqref{l4-3-1} and the fact that for any $x,y,z\in \mathds R^d$ with $|x-y|\geqslant 5t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}$ and $z \in B(x,t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}})$ and for every $0<t\leqslant 1$, \begin{align*} |x-y|^{-d-\alpha(z)}&\succeq |x-y|^{-d-\alpha(x)+C_2|x-z|^{\beta_0}}\succeq t^{C_2t^{{\beta_0}/{\alpha_1}}}|x-y|^{-d-\alpha(x)}\succeq |x-y|^{-d-\alpha(x)}. \end{align*} According to \eqref{t4-4-2}, \eqref{t4-4-3} and \eqref{t4-4-4}, we obtain that for any $|x-y|>5t^{{1}/{\alpha(x)}}$ and $\lambda$ small enough, \begin{equation} \mathds P_x\big(X_{\lambda t}\in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})\big)\succeq \frac{t^{1+({d}/{\alpha(y)})}}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha(x)}}. \end{equation} Hence, we arrive at \begin{align*} p(t,x,y)&=\int_{\mathds R^d}p(\lambda t,x,z)p((1-\lambda)t,z,y)\,dz\\ &\geqslant \int_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})} p(\lambda t,x,z)p((1-\lambda)t,z,y)\,dz\\ &\geqslant \inf_{|z-y|\leqslant t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}}p((1-\lambda)t,z,y) \int_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})}p(\lambda t,x,z)\,dz\\ &\succeq \inf_{|z-y|\leqslant C_3t^{{1}/{\alpha(z)}}}p((1-\lambda)t,z,y) \int_{B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})}p(\lambda t,x,z)\,dz\\ &\succeq t^{-{d}/{\alpha(y)}} \mathds P_x\big(X_{\lambda t}\in B(y,t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}})\big)\succeq \frac{t}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha(x)}}, \end{align*} where the third inequality follows from the fact that $t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}\asymp t^{{1}/{\alpha(z)}}$ for every $|y-z|\leqslant t^{{1}/{\alpha(y)}}$, in the forth inequality we used \eqref{p4-3-1}, and in the last inequality we used \eqref{t4-4-5}. Therefore, \eqref{t4-4-1} has been proved.
